report.source_text: Three weeks post-surgery, a significant improvement was noted in the vitreous reaction. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a whitish scar in the superior and temporal regions of the optic disc, accompanied by a persistent macular star (figure 5). At 6 weeks postoperation, the macula status remained similar to that observed at the third week postoperation, with a reduction in the hard exudates (figure 6). BCVA in the right eye had improved to 6/9, indicating a successful outcome in managing the intracameral gnathostomiasis presenting as neuroretinitis.

Consequently, albendazole at a dosage of 400 mg two times per day was initiated for a 21-day course.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Intraocular gnathostomiasis (Gnathostoma spinigerum infection) presenting as neuroretinitis/panuveitis
clinician.trajectory_summary: A male in his 40s presented with acute unilateral panuveitis and neuroretinitis (optic disc edema, macular edema, vitritis) with peripheral eosinophilia (8%). Initial infectious workup was negative for HIV, syphilis, TB, and Bartonella. Brain CT showed no intraocular parasites. One week after initiation of topical corticosteroids, slit-lamp examination revealed a live nematode in the anterior chamber with associated iris changes. The nematode was surgically extracted and sent to Microbiology, where it was identified as Gnathostoma spinigerum (5 mm × 0.5 mm) based on morphological characteristics including a head bulb, cuticular spines, and internal structures (intestinal tract, cervical sac, oesophagus). Post-operatively, the patient received topical and oral corticosteroids plus a 21-day course of albendazole (400 mg BID) starting on postoperative day 7. The clinical course showed progressive resolution of intraocular inflammation, with BCVA improving from 6/60 at presentation to 6/9 by 6 weeks post-surgery, accompanied by disc scarring and persistent macular star.
